Who drank more alcohol, and what will sober them up?","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"They drank about the same half ounce of alcohol, and only time will sober them up.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Those servings each hold about the same half ounce of alcohol, and only time sobers a person up, so quick tricks fail.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Alcohol and the driver","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alcohol changes judgment and skill.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F03"]},{"text":"Only time sobers you up.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Welcome to the lesson on how alcohol affects a driver. The New Jersey manual is direct about this topic. Alcohol can make a driver overconfident and unable to think clearly, and even a small amount raises the chance of a crash. In this lesson you will see which driving skills start to slip after a few drinks, why alcohol paired with anger is so dangerous, and why most alcohol-related crashes hurt more people than the driver. You will also learn why only time sobers a person up, and how a serving of whiskey, a serving of beer and a serving of wine compare. Keep these ideas together, because each one builds on the last.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Overconfident and not thinking clearly","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alcohol can breed overconfidence.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Clear thinking slips.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"A small amount raises crash risk.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Alcohol with anger fuels reckless driving.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the mind. Alcohol can make a driver overconfident and unable to think clearly. That is a dangerous mix, because the driver feels more able at the very moment they are less able. The manual adds that even a small amount of alcohol raises the chance of a crash, and that holds even when the driver believes they are under the legal limit. Now add emotion. The manual says alcohol paired with anger accounts for much of the reckless, aggressive driving behind fatal highway crashes. So a driver who has been drinking and is also angry brings together the two forces the manual links to reckless, aggressive driving and fatal highway crashes.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Skills that start to slip","fact_ids":["sec10-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two, three or four drinks.","fact_ids":["sec10-F02"]},{"text":"Reaction time, coordination and balance suffer.","fact_ids":["sec10-F02"]},{"text":"Vision and distance judgment dull.","fact_ids":["sec10-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Next come the physical skills. According to the manual, after two, three or four drinks, alcohol starts to impair reaction time, coordination and balance. It also dulls vision and the ability to judge distance. That is five abilities hit by one cause: reaction time, coordination, balance, vision and the ability to judge distance, all from the same few drinks. Notice also that the manual does not set this at some huge amount. Two, three or four drinks is where the trouble starts. If a question asks which abilities alcohol affects, look for reaction time, coordination, balance, vision and judging distance.","fact_ids":["sec10-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"One vehicle, many victims","fact_ids":["sec10-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Most alcohol crashes involve one vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec10-F04"]},{"text":"They often kill or seriously injure several people.","fact_ids":["sec10-F04"]},{"text":"Passengers, pedestrians and other drivers.","fact_ids":["sec10-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a fact worth slowing down on. Most alcohol-related crashes involve a single vehicle. You might expect that to mean only the drinking driver gets hurt, but the manual says the opposite. These crashes often kill or seriously injure several people, including passengers, pedestrians and other drivers. In other words, one impaired driver in one car can still put many lives at risk. The people riding along, the people walking nearby and the people driving past did not choose to drink, yet they share the danger. Keep both halves of the fact together: a single vehicle is usually involved, yet several people are often hurt or killed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"No quick way to sober up","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Only time sobers a person up.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]},{"text":"The liver burns off about ninety percent.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]},{"text":"The rest leaves through breath, urine and sweat.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]},{"text":"Quick sober-up tricks fail.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Now for a common trap. It is tempting to believe there is a fast way to sober up before driving. The manual says there is not. Only time sobers a person up. The liver burns off about ninety percent of the alcohol, and the other ten percent leaves the body through breath, urine and sweat. That is exactly why quick sober-up tricks fail: the process takes time, and a trick cannot stand in for it. So if a question offers a shortcut, any shortcut, as the way to become fit to drive after drinking, treat it as the wrong answer. The only answer the manual accepts is time, and nothing a driver drinks or does will replace it.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":47,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Whiskey, beer and wine compared","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Whiskey: one and a half ounces, eighty-proof.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]},{"text":"Beer: twelve ounces.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]},{"text":"Wine: five ounces.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]},{"text":"Each holds about a half ounce of alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"It is easy to assume that beer or wine is a gentler choice than hard liquor. The manual compares servings to show why that idea fails. One and a half ounces of eighty-proof whiskey, twelve ounces of beer and five ounces of wine each hold about the same half ounce of alcohol. So a serving of beer is not a lighter drink when it comes to alcohol. The manual also cites studies showing that beer is what most drivers arrested for drunk driving had been drinking. Put those two facts side by side: a beer carries about the same alcohol as the other servings, and beer is the drink most often behind those arrests.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Whiskey or beer?","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Jordan: whiskey. Who is over the legal limit, and how great is the crash risk?","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-F10"]},"answer":{"text":"Both are over the limit, and the crash risk is six times as great.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-F10"]},"rationale":{"text":"Zero point one zero is above the adult zero point zero eight and the under-twenty-one zero point zero one, and crash risk is six times as great at that level.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F10"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Measuring alcohol and the limits","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"BAC measures how much is too much.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-R02"]},{"text":"Two legal limits in New Jersey.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-R02"]},{"text":"Crash risk climbs with BAC.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson turns alcohol into numbers you can use. The manual says blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is the only scientific measure of how much is too much, and a simple breath test reveals it. You will learn the four factors that decide a person's BAC, what food can and cannot do, and the two New Jersey legal limits, one for adults and one for drivers under twenty-one. Then you will see how crash risk climbs as BAC rises, from double, to six times, to twenty-five times as great. Listen closely to the numbers, because several of them sound alike and they are easy to swap under pressure.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F07","sec10-F08","sec10-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"BAC and the breath test","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"BAC means blood alcohol concentration.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},{"text":"The only scientific measure of too much.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},{"text":"A simple breath test reveals it.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},{"text":"Four factors set it.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the measure itself. Notice that body weight is on the list, so the same drinks will not always mean the same BAC for two different people. Food slows how fast alcohol enters the blood, but it cannot prevent a high BAC during steady heavy drinking, and it does not make anyone sober. Put another way, eating slows alcohol absorption, but heavy drinking always produces a high BAC whatever was eaten. So food changes the speed, not the outcome. First, what happens when a driver refuses a breath test in New Jersey.
